opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated parts of doing safety work inside a frontier lab. Influence there isn't something you get by being right in the abstract. You get it by being useful. If I go to a product team or a capabilities team and say, "Here's a technique that matters for some hypothetical future system that's much smarter than anything we have," that's a hard sell. People are busy, they have deadlines, and they reasonably want evidence that something works on real problems now.

But if I can find a technique that does both, say a probe that catches a model behaving badly in some way the team already cares about, like hallucinating, being sycophantic, or ignoring instructions, and that same technique is something I think will scale to detecting deception or misalignment in more capable systems, then everyone wins. The team gets something that solves their current headache. I get the technique stress-tested on real models at real scale, with real feedback, which is far more informative than toy settings. And it builds trust and relationships, so the next time I come with something that's more speculative, people actually listen.

There's also an epistemic benefit I care about. Safety research can drift into things that look clever but never touch reality. When you're forced to show your method helps on a concrete problem today, you get a fast feedback loop that keeps you honest. A lot of interpretability techniques that seemed promising turned out to be beaten by simple baselines once we tried them on practical tasks, and learning that early is really valuable.

And practically, the infrastructure tends to persist. If a monitoring tool gets built into the real pipeline because it's useful now, then when the stakes get higher it's already there, it's been debugged, and people know how to use it. That's much better than trying to bolt something on in a crisis.

I don't want to overstate it. Sometimes the overlap isn't there, and you need to do work that only pays off for AGI safety and argue for it on its own merits. But I think people underrate how often the overlap exists if you look for it, and how much leverage you get from pursuing it.

r001.rationale: The response says product and capabilities teams can adopt techniques that solve current problems, helping build them into real workflows while also supporting long-term safety.

r002.rationale: It describes useful safety techniques becoming part of real pipelines, but does not compare modifying an existing practice with adding an entirely new component.

r003.rationale: It says busy teams are more receptive to techniques that solve current problems, but does not say that presenting an already implemented change is easier than asking engineers to implement a proposed idea.

fable-5.1.text:
Neel Nanda: So I think the honest answer is that it's a mix of pragmatism and genuine intellectual humility. When I'm working inside a lab, the people around me are mostly not thinking about superintelligence on a daily basis. They're thinking about "why does this model refuse things it shouldn't?" or "why did fine-tuning on this dataset make the model weirdly sycophantic?" or "can we tell whether this model is actually using the reasoning it wrote down?" And these are real problems they need solved this quarter.

Now, my worry historically with interpretability was that it could become this very isolated research programme, where you do beautiful work on toy models and then it just never touches anything that matters. And I think the single best check against that is: can you actually help someone with a problem they already have? If your technique can't shed any light on the models people are shipping today, that's at least weak evidence that it won't shed light on the models that are actually dangerous either. Because the dangerous models are going to be continuous with the current ones in a lot of ways.

The other thing is that I've just become more sceptical of my own ability to predict in advance which techniques will matter. Like, if you'd asked me three years ago, I'd have said we need to fully reverse engineer circuits, and the stuff about probes and steering was kind of a side-show. And now I think probes are probably one of the most useful things we have, precisely because they're cheap and they work on frontier models. So having a feedback loop where colleagues tell you "this was useful" or "this was useless" is incredibly valuable for correcting those kinds of mistakes.

And then there's a slightly cynical point, which is that resources follow usefulness. If interpretability is seen as the team that helps everyone debug their models, you get compute, you get headcount, you get people wanting to collaborate with you. If it's seen as this abstract thing that a few people care about for philosophical reasons, that's a lot harder to sustain. And I do think it's important that we go into the period where things get really dangerous with a lot of people who actually have experience looking inside models, rather than a handful of us.

The thing I try to be careful about is not letting the short-term stuff completely eat the long-term stuff. There's a version of this where you just become a debugging service and never ask the harder questions about deception or whether we can trust a model's stated reasoning. So I think of it more as: find the overlap, work hard on the overlap, but keep some explicit budget for the bets that only make sense if you take AGI seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says lab colleagues focused on current, non-safety problems can help assess and use interpretability techniques, while work on today’s models may also apply to dangerous future models.

r002.rationale: It argues for finding overlap with existing needs, but does not compare adopting a safety-relevant modification to an existing practice with adopting an entirely new component.

r003.rationale: It discusses helping colleagues with current problems, but does not say that handing them an implemented change makes adoption easier than asking them to implement a proposal.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s much easier to do useful research when there’s a real feedback loop. If a colleague has a problem they care about today, and an interpretability technique helps them solve it, that gives you evidence that the technique is actually useful. They’ll try it, tell you where it breaks, and push you to make it better.

That doesn’t mean solving today’s problems automatically translates into making AGI safe. You still need an argument for why the thing you’re developing will matter as models become more capable. But if you can find that overlap, you get both a reason to care about the research in the long term and a way to test whether you’re making progress now.

There’s also a straightforward collaboration benefit: people are more excited to work with you if you’re helping with something they already care about. You don’t need everyone to share your entire view of the future to do valuable work together.

r001.rationale: The response says colleagues focused on present-day problems may try an interpretability technique that helps them, and connects that technique to long-term AGI safety.

r002.rationale: It does not compare modifying an existing practice with introducing an entirely new component.

r003.rationale: It does not say the change is already implemented or compare that with asking engineers to implement a proposed idea.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of useful research happens when you find a question that makes sense from several different perspectives. If someone wants to understand why their model is behaving strangely, and I think the techniques we develop to investigate that might eventually help us understand whether a much more capable model is deceiving us, there’s a real opportunity to work together.

One reason I value that is that feedback from concrete problems is incredibly useful. It’s easy to have a story about why your research will help with AGI safety, but if the only test is whether it sounds plausible, you can fool yourself. Having colleagues who want your tools to explain something they actually care about gives you a more demanding test of whether those tools work.

And it means you can benefit from people who have different motivations and expertise. They don’t need to agree with my whole picture of the future to contribute something valuable. The caveat is that usefulness today doesn’t automatically imply usefulness for AGI safety. You still need to think carefully about that connection. But where there’s genuine overlap, I think it’s worth looking for it.

r001.rationale: The response says colleagues with different motivations can contribute valuable expertise, but does not clearly state that people pursuing goals unrelated to safety can drive implementation of safety techniques.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare adopting a safety modification to an existing practice with adopting an entirely new component.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that providing an implemented change makes adoption easier than asking busy engineers to implement an idea.
